metaDescription: Six push reel mowers compared on width, blade count, wheel design and weight, with guidance for small lawns, tight yards and low-cut turf.
expertTake: The LawnMaster LMRM1801 is the pick for a mid-size lawn that needs a wide cut and fine height control, and the American Lawn Mower 1304-14SK2 is the pick for a small yard with a sharpener included. Households with long grass, steep banks or more than a few thousand square feet to cover should look at a powered mower instead.
introParagraphs: Pushing a human-powered mower is a different experience from steering a motor. The wheels drive the reel directly, so every foot you walk spins the blades, and the machine only cuts well at a steady walking pace.

That direct link makes the details of wheels, handle and weight matter more than they do on a powered mower. The six models here span narrow lightweight designs for small plots and a wide four-wheel design for longer runs, so the choice depends on how much ground you cover and how tightly you turn.

products.name: LawnMaster LMRM1801 18-Inch 5-Blade Push Reel Mower
products.description:
The LMRM1801 is the sweet spot of the group: an 18 inch deck wide enough to save passes, narrow enough to turn around beds, and nine cutting positions to tune the height. The maker pitches it at small lawns, which matches its effort level.

Ten inch front wheels roll over leaves and small bumps that stall smaller wheels, and the five-blade reel gives a scissor cut that avoids the ripped tips of an impact blade. Against the LawnMaster 14 inch it covers nearly a third more ground per pass, though it pushes harder, and against the Garvee 18 inch it keeps the conventional two-wheel layout that most users find more predictable.

Expect to adjust the reel contact when the mower arrives, because hardware seats in over the first few mows. Rinse clippings away, oil the pivots and sharpen every year or two. It stores upright in a shed corner.
products.bestFor: A small to medium lawn where fine height control and an 18 inch swath both matter.
pros: 18 inch width balances coverage and handling
Nine height positions for fine adjustment
10 inch front wheels ride over bumps
Scissor action avoids shredded grass tips
cons: Harder to push than the 14 inch models
Minimum height is too high for very short turf

products.name: American Lawn Mower 1204-14 14-Inch 4-Blade Push Reel Mower
products.description:
The 1204-14 is the lightest design here: four blades on a 14 inch reel with 8.5 inch polymer wheels. It cuts from half an inch to 1.75 inches and is rated to handle grass up to 4 inches tall, which makes it forgiving of a missed week.

Four blades push very easily, and that is its appeal for older users or anyone who finds a seven-blade reel hard work. The compromise is a coarser cut than a five-blade reel, and the small wheels are less tolerant of lumpy ground. Compared with the 4-blade 2204-14 it is the older design with the smaller wheels.

Lubricate the pivots, keep the reel clear of twigs and expect to sharpen every couple of seasons. Store it with the blades clean and dry.
products.bestFor: A small flat yard where light weight and easy pushing matter most.
pros: Four blades push very easily
Cuts as low as half an inch
Handles grass up to 4 inches tall
Light polymer wheels and frame
cons: Small 8.5 inch wheels ride bumps poorly
Fewer blades give a coarser cut

products.name: American Lawn Mower 1304-14SK2 14-Inch 5-Blade Reel with Sharpener
products.description:
The 1304-14SK2 pairs a five-blade 14 inch reel with 10 inch polymer wheels and a hand sharpener in the box. A sharpener turns a once-in-a-while chore into a ten-minute job you do yourself.

It cuts from 1 to 2.25 inches, a range that suits cool-season grass at a healthy summer height better than the 0.5 inch floor of the 1204-14. Five blades give a smoother cut than four, and the larger wheels roll better on uneven turf.

Use the sharpener when the cut starts to look torn at the tips, not when it stalls. Wipe the reel clean after each mow and check contact each spring. It is the best long-term value for a small yard.
products.bestFor: A small lawn owner who wants to maintain the blades at home.
pros: Hand sharpener included in the box
Five blades give a clean scissor cut
10 inch wheels roll over minor bumps
1 to 2.25 inch range suits cool-season grass

products.name: American Lawn Mower 2204-14 14-Inch 4-Blade Push Reel Mower
products.description:
The 2204-14 is a four-blade, 14 inch machine with a cushion-grip T-handle. The T handle sits higher and gives a comfortable two-hand grip, which helps if you find a straight tube handle tiring.

Its cutting range runs from half an inch to 1.75 inches, so it suits short, regularly mowed turf rather than tall lawns. It is a routine-maintenance machine: cut weekly and it works well, let the grass go and it will struggle. Against the 1204-14 it has the same blade count and range but a newer handle design.

Keep the reel adjusted, lubricate the pivots and keep the blades free of clippings. Store it dry.
products.bestFor: A short, weekly-mowed lawn where handle comfort matters.
pros: Cushion-grip T handle is comfortable
Four blades push easily
Cuts from half an inch
Light and easy to store
cons: Four blades give a less fine finish

products.name: LawnMaster LMRM1401 14-Inch 5-Blade Push Reel Mower
products.description:
The LMRM1401 narrows the LawnMaster design to 14 inches with four height positions starting at an inch. It keeps the 10 inch front wheels of the larger models, which is where the machine earns its place against similar narrow mowers.

Four positions is a coarser adjustment than the nine on the LMRM1801, so you pick from a few presets rather than tuning by quarter inches. The five-blade reel pushes easier than a seven-blade one and handles ordinary grass. It is easy to lift into a car or a shed.

Rinse clippings off, keep the axles lubricated and check the reel contact. It fits tight spaces such as a courtyard or a front strip.
products.bestFor: A courtyard or front lawn where tight turns beat coverage.
pros: Narrow body turns easily
10 inch front wheels ride bumps
Five blades give a scissor cut
Easy to carry and store

products.name: Garvee 18-Inch 4-Wheel 5-Blade Push Reel Mower
products.description:
The Garvee puts four wheels under an 18 inch deck, which spreads the weight and keeps the reel level over flat ground. A carbon steel frame and reinforced ABS parts carry the load.

Four wheels improve balance and make the mower steady, but they also add rolling resistance and make tight pivots harder than on a two-wheel design. It is a newer brand with less track record than American Lawn Mower or LawnMaster, so parts and support are less certain.

Check the reel contact on arrival, since a four-wheel frame may arrive slightly out of square. Keep the wheels clear of grass and sharpen the blades when the cut degrades.
products.bestFor: A flat lawn where stability matters more than tight turning.
pros: Four wheels keep the reel level
18 inch cut covers ground quickly
Carbon steel frame for strength
Five-blade reel for a clean cut
cons: Newer brand with less parts support
Four wheels are harder to pivot

buyingCriteria.explanation: Every extra inch of width adds resistance, because more blade is chewing grass at once. The LawnMaster LMRM1801 and Garvee at 18 inches cover the most ground, while the 14 inch American Lawn Mower and LawnMaster models are easiest to push. If you have a bad shoulder or a sloping yard, pick the narrow machine and accept the extra passes. A quick way to judge is to count your passes: a 40 foot lawn width takes about thirty passes with a 14 inch reel and about twenty-three with an 18 inch one, and the shorter job has to be paid for with a heavier push on every pass. Many owners find the narrow machine finishes sooner in practice because they stop less often.

Reel mowers are driven by their wheels, so a wheel that stalls on a root stops the reel. Ten inch wheels on the LawnMaster and American 1304-14SK2 ride bumps better than the 8.5 inch wheels on the 1204-14. A four-wheel design like the Garvee spreads load but resists turning. Walk your lawn first and check for dips. Roots, gopher mounds and the lip where a driveway meets turf are the usual stoppers, and each one is a place where the wheel lifts and the reel stops spinning. Filling a low spot with topsoil costs less than a mower with bigger wheels, and a lawn rolled flat in spring makes any reel mower cut better.

Four blades push easily and suit light, frequent mowing, as on the American 1204-14 and 2204-14. Five blades give a finer cut on the LawnMaster, Garvee and American 1304-14SK2 at a cost in effort. Seven blades are for fine turf and are not in this guide. Choose the blade count your arms can sustain across the whole lawn. The extra blade also changes how the mower behaves in thicker growth: a five-blade reel sheds clippings in finer pieces that fall into the lawn, while a four-blade reel leaves slightly longer clippings that are more visible on a dry day. Neither is a problem, but it explains why two mowers with the same width can feel quite different in the hand.

The American 1204-14 and 2204-14 cut from half an inch to 1.75 inches, which suits short turf but not a cool-season lawn kept at 3 inches. The 1304-14SK2 runs 1 to 2.25 inches and the LawnMaster LMRM1801 has nine positions. Match the range to the grass height you actually keep. Cool-season grasses such as bluegrass and fescue do best at 2.5 inches or more through summer heat, which is above what the American 1204-14 and 2204-14 can reach, while warm-season turf is happier cut short. Cutting more than a third of the blade at once stresses grass, so the top setting also sets how long you can leave it between mows.

A reel mower pushes from the handle, so a comfortable grip reduces fatigue. The American 2204-14 uses a cushion-grip T handle that places hands higher. Taller users may prefer a higher T, and shorter users a straight handle. Try different grips if you can, because a mower that fits your hands is mowed more often.

Reel blades dull slowly but misalignment shows up fast. The American 1304-14SK2 ships with a hand sharpener, which saves a service visit. Without one you will use lapping compound or pay a shop. Wipe the reel after each mow and oil the pivots.

howWeEvaluated.title: Push effort
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed width, blade count and wheel design together as a measure of effort. The four-blade 14 inch American models are easiest, and the 18 inch machines hardest.

howWeEvaluated.title: Terrain handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared wheel diameter and layout. Ten inch wheels on the LawnMaster and American 1304-14SK2 score above the 8.5 inch wheels on the 1204-14.

howWeEvaluated.title: Height flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared range and the number of positions. The LawnMaster LMRM1801 with nine positions leads for fine control.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted an included sharpener and common service parts. The American 1304-14SK2 scores best, with the less proven Garvee lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed handle design, weight and balance. The cushion T handle of the 2204-14 and the light 1204-14 body score highest.

cards.label: Four blades
cards.text: The American 1204-14 and 2204-14 use four blades. They push easily and suit short, frequent mowing, but leave a slightly coarser cut.

cards.label: Five blades
cards.text: The LawnMaster models, Garvee and American 1304-14SK2 use five. They cut finer and tolerate more grass height at a modest cost in effort.

howToChoose.note: Choose four blades for effort, five blades for finish.

rows: Cuts down to half an inch

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a light mower you can lift, large front wheels, and a width that fits your tightest gap. A small yard is mostly turning, so agility matters more than swath.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The LawnMaster LMRM1401 and American 1304-14SK2 are the two best fits, with the sharpener giving the American a longer service life.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you want fine height control and a wide cut, as on the LawnMaster LMRM1801. A wide, well-adjusted mower saves real time each week.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if your lawn is small and flat. The American 1204-14 or 2204-14 does the job, as long as you mow weekly.

maintenance.why: Blades should just kiss the bedknife. Too tight drags and too loose leaves uncut strips.
A hand sharpener or lapping compound restores a clean cut before tips turn brown.

Wet clippings cake between blades and a twig can jam the reel. A stiff brush or a hose clears the reel in a minute, and letting it dry before storage prevents rust forming on the bedknife edge. Walk the lawn before mowing and pick up sticks, toys and acorns, because the bedknife is the part that gets nicked.
Dry joints raise push effort and stiffen the height adjuster.

Worn or loose wheels slip and stall the reel. Tighten axle nuts and replace cracked wheels. The wheels drive the reel through a gear or pawl, so a wheel that spins without turning the reel means the drive has worn or filled with grit. Cleaning and lubricating the drive end usually fixes it, and it is worth checking before you assume the mower needs replacing.

faq.q: Is a push reel mower hard to use?
faq.a: Narrow four-blade models push easily on flat ground. Wider five-blade machines take more effort, and all of them need a steady walking pace to spin the reel.

faq.q: How tall can the grass be?
faq.a: Most are happiest below the height setting, about 2 inches for the models here. The American 1204-14 is rated to handle grass up to 4 inches, but cut tall grass in stages.

faq.q: Do I need a motor for a larger lawn?
faq.a: Past about a fifth of an acre the effort and time add up quickly. A powered mower or a robotic mower is more practical.

Reels are best on flat ground. On slopes the wheels slip and traction drops, and the mower tends to pull sideways. If you must mow a gentle slope, mow across it rather than up and down, keep the grass dry and take narrower passes. A steep bank is a job for a string trimmer, not a reel mower.

faq.q: Why does the mower leave tufts?
faq.a: Usually out-of-adjustment blades, a dull reel or grass too tall for the setting. Adjust contact first, then sharpen.
It is possible but clumps clippings and clogs the reel. Wait until the lawn is dry for the cleanest cut.
